clue.text: Around Tyneside, suits will get perks

indicators.note: 'around' tells us one word is wrapped about the other, so the second clue element encloses the first

blocks.note: to suit something is to befit it
Tyneside is in the North East of England, abbreviated NE

explanation.surface: Workers in the North East are promised that their suits come with extra perks.
explanation.walkthrough: Tyneside, around Newcastle, lies in North East England, which crosswords shorten to NE.
explanation.definitionFit: Benefits are the extras that come with a job, which is exactly what perks are.

clue.text: Beelzebub, bleeding, hiding blister

indicators.note: the two neighbouring clue words are said to be hiding something, so the letters lie concealed across them

blocks.note: the end of the first name runs into the start of the next word

explanation.surface: The devil himself, wounded and bleeding, is concealing a painful sore.
explanation.definitionFit: A bubble is a raised pocket on a surface, as a blister is on skin or paint.

clue.text: Not a single store had food

blocks.note: not a single one means none, NO
a shed is a place to store things

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper laments that no shop had anything to eat.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'store had food' together; the definition is only the last two words.
explanation.definitionFit: To nosh is informal slang for eating, so having noshed means one has eaten a meal.

clue.text: Maths whiz, wonderfully fab, iconic

indicators.note: something done wonderfully is done with flair, inviting the letters to be rearranged freely

blocks.note: the two words supply all the letters

explanation.surface: A tribute to a brilliant mathematician, gushing that the genius is fab and iconic.
explanation.definitionFit: Fibonacci was a medieval Italian mathematician, famous for the number sequence named after him.

clue.text: It might be presented as cheetah in that titfer, for starters!

definitions.text: It might be presented as cheetah in that titfer, for starters!

indicators.note: starters are what come first, so only the opening letter of the word before is taken
presenting the letters in another form invites rearranging them into a new phrase

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of titfer

explanation.surface: A playful retitling of a famous children's book: a big cat wearing that hat.
explanation.walkthrough: Titfer is Cockney rhyming slang for hat (tit-for-tat), so 'cheetah in that titfer' is also a jokey paraphrase of the title itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cat in the Hat is the Dr Seuss picture book, and a cheetah wearing a hat literally describes its title.

clue.text: In France, who gets behind cook (not French) offering French dish?

indicators.note: 'not French' asks us to drop the abbreviation for French from the word for cook

blocks.note: qui is the French word for who
a chef is a cook
F is the abbreviation for French

explanation.surface: A puzzle about who assists the chef in a French kitchen serving a national dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets behind' places the cook's word after the French word; CHEF loses its F.
explanation.definitionFit: A quiche is a savoury egg-custard tart from Lorraine, a classic dish of French cuisine.

clue.text: Employers in trouser suits

indicators.note: 'in' tells us the letters sit inside the following words rather than being built

blocks.note: found running from inside the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Bosses who turn up to work dressed in trouser suits.
explanation.definitionFit: One who employs something makes use of it, so users of a tool are its employers.

clue.text: Swindle very cunningly, snatching old type of belt

indicators.note: doing something cunningly suggests twisting it, so the letters of the word before get rearranged
to snatch is to grab and hold, so one piece takes another inside it

blocks.note: a con is a swindle
taken as written
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A crafty fraudster pulls off a scam and grabs a vintage belt as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Belt' looks like something the swindler steals; it belongs to the definition, which needs 'type of' to fit.
explanation.definitionFit: A conveyor belt is a moving band carrying goods along, so this is one particular kind of belt.

clue.text: Illustrative warnings make Max sleep fitfully

indicators.note: sleeping fitfully means tossing and turning, so the letters toss about into a new order

blocks.note: the name and the verb supply all the letters

explanation.surface: Cautionary tales give poor Max nightmares, so he tosses and turns at night.
explanation.definitionFit: To make an example of someone is to punish them as a deterrent, so examples can serve as cautionary lessons.

clue.text: In this arrangement, we might see dingo anger them!

definitions.text: In this arrangement, we might see dingo anger them!

indicators.note: an arrangement puts things in a fresh order, so the following letters are reordered

blocks.note: three words supply all the letters

explanation.surface: A wild dog stirs up trouble for the animals around it.
explanation.walkthrough: In Aesop's fable the dog lies in the cattle's manger, eating no hay itself but snarling them away, which certainly angers them.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog in the manger selfishly keeps from others something it cannot use, angering them, just as the fable's dog does.

clue.text: Go-getter policeman given basic spelling test

blocks.note: busy is old British slang for a detective or police officer
a spelling bee is a spelling contest, and bee is its basic word

explanation.surface: An ambitious officer sits a simple spelling test.
explanation.walkthrough: BUSY is British underworld slang for a police officer, especially a detective.
explanation.definitionFit: A busy bee is an energetic, industrious person, much like an ambitious go-getter always on the move.

clue.text: ‘Dancing On Ice: 'Australia’ vacuously presenting ‘Polynesia, etc’

indicators.note: emptied out, the country's name keeps only its outer shell with its middle gone
letters that are dancing move around and change places

blocks.note: taken as written
just the first and last letters of the country

explanation.surface: A TV skating show gets an Australian edition with an empty-headed host showing off the Pacific islands.
explanation.walkthrough: Dancing On Ice is a British TV show where celebrities learn to figure skate.
explanation.definitionFit: Oceania is the region of Pacific islands including Polynesia, Melanesia, Micronesia and Australasia.

clue.text: Dishonesty concerning time spent with crossword, perhaps

blocks.note: a lie is an act of dishonesty
in can mean concerning, as in 'in this matter'

explanation.surface: Someone fibs about how long they spend on the daily crossword.
explanation.definitionFit: A lie-in is a lazy morning staying in bed, often spent leisurely with the paper and its puzzle.

clue.text: Slightly inclined to be a little dear

blocks.note: first meaning: a slope rising somewhat sharply
second meaning: a price that is rather high

explanation.surface: Someone half-tempted to be sweet and affectionate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inclined' and 'dear' pretend to be about mood and affection; they are a gradient and a price.
explanation.definitionFit: Steep describes both a sharp gradient and an excessive price, and the softener fits either sense.

clue.text: A German in each hotel — being prepared is hidden strength

indicators.note: something prepared has been worked over, like ingredients, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: ein is German for a
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A German tourist in every hotel, always ready, has a secret reserve of strength.
explanation.definitionFit: In stud poker the face-down ace is a concealed winning card, hence any secret advantage held in reserve.

clue.text: Sturgeon’s aim: Scotland finally off, a natural process

indicators.note: 'finally' points to the closing letter of the nation's name
'off' means removed, so that letter is taken away from the aim

blocks.note: Nicola Sturgeon, former Scottish First Minister, campaigned for power passing from London to Scotland
the final letter of Scotland

explanation.surface: A Scottish politician's goal is for Scotland to break away, which she presents as natural.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sturgeon' looks like the fish; it is Nicola Sturgeon, who led Scotland's government. DEVOLUTION loses its D.
explanation.definitionFit: Evolution is the gradual development of species by natural selection, a process occurring in nature.

clue.text: Ousting when Liberal drops back two places in poll

indicators.note: moving back two places in the alphabet swaps one letter for the one two steps earlier

blocks.note: a poll is an election
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A party is thrown out when the Liberal vote slips two places in the polls.
explanation.walkthrough: L stepping back through K lands on J, so the poll word changes its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ejection is the act of throwing someone out, the same as ousting them from a place or post.

clue.text: Half of mush to percolate and circulate

indicators.note: taking only half of a word means discarding the other half of its letters

blocks.note: schmaltz is excessive sentimentality, mush
to ooze is to seep slowly through, like percolating liquid

explanation.surface: Instructions for making coffee: half the grounds, let it percolate, then pour round.
explanation.walkthrough: SCHMALTZ has eight letters; its front four, SCHM, join OOZE.
explanation.definitionFit: To schmooze is to chat ingratiatingly at a social gathering, mingling as one moves around a room.

clue.text: Give up TV? It’s child’s play

definitions.note: here a child's plaything, not something easy

blocks.note: to jack in is British slang for to quit
the box is informal for the television

explanation.surface: Turning off the television is easy, any child could do it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Child's play' wants to mean something easy; it is a toy. Jack in is British slang for quitting.
explanation.definitionFit: A jack-in-the-box is a toy where a puppet springs from a box, a plaything for little ones.

clue.text: Mickey Mouse's company with a lot invested

indicators.note: money invested is put into something, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
a heap is a lot of something

explanation.surface: Disney's company has had a large sum put into it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mickey Mouse' reads as the Disney character; it is the adjective for shoddy, and 's means is.
explanation.definitionFit: As slang, Mickey Mouse describes something trivial or shoddy, much like something cheap and poor in quality.

clue.text: Incompetently seared, destroyed the lot

indicators.note: something done incompetently is botched, so the letters end up jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A clumsy cook burnt the steaks and ruined the whole batch.
explanation.definitionFit: To erase is to wipe out completely, so erased means wiped everything out, leaving nothing remaining.

clue.text: ’Spare mo’ with Cameron? It’s lasted centuries

indicators.note: to go spare is British slang for going wild with anger, so the letters go wild

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks a politician named Cameron to spare a moment, and is told something has gone on for ages.
explanation.definitionFit: The Common Era is the secular name for the dating system counted from year one, now about two thousand years long.

clue.text: No livery includes a yellowish green

indicators.note: the phrase is said to include something, so the letters are held within it

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A uniform rule: no livery may feature a yellowish green colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Olive is the dull yellow-green shade of an unripe olive, so it names this colour.

clue.text: Wedding guide more sumptuous with outlay of pounds

indicators.note: an outlay is money laid out and gone, so that item is spent from the word

blocks.note: lush means luxurious, so more lush is more sumptuous
L is the abbreviation for pounds, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A lavish wedding guide that costs a lot more money.
explanation.walkthrough: LUSHER loses its L to leave USHER.
explanation.definitionFit: At a wedding an usher shows guests to their seats in the church, guiding them on arrival.

clue.text: Primarily, it’s where old Japanese infantry met Americans?

definitions.text: Primarily, it’s where old Japanese infantry met Americans?

indicators.note: 'primarily' means first of all, so the first letter of each following word is used

blocks.clueFragment: it’s where old Japanese infantry met Americans
blocks.note: the opening letters of the seven words

explanation.surface: A history question about where Japanese soldiers fought the US.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue both supplies the letters and describes the place.
explanation.definitionFit: Iwo Jima is the Pacific island where US Marines fought Japanese troops in a famous 1945 battle.

clue.text: What might be plucked, when it’s dipped in refined sugar

indicators.note: refining something processes it into another form, so the letters are reworked
something dipped in goes inside, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something like a strawberry being dipped in sugar before it is picked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plucked' suggests fruit or poultry; it is strings.
explanation.definitionFit: Guitars are stringed instruments whose strings are plucked with fingers or a pick to make sound.

clue.text: English seen in Riviera city society with family

definitions.note: a collective noun for plural relatives

indicators.note: 'seen in' places one thing inside another, so a letter sits within the city

blocks.note: Nice is a city on the French Riviera
E is the abbreviation for English
S is the abbreviation for society

explanation.surface: English visitors spotted among the high society of a Riviera resort with their relatives.
explanation.definitionFit: Nieces are relatives, daughters of one's brothers or sisters, and so members of one's kin.

clue.text: Victorian novel Conrad frequently reinvented

indicators.note: something reinvented is made over in a new shape, so the letters take a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
FR is the abbreviation for frequently

explanation.surface: Joseph Conrad keeps rewriting a nineteenth-century novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conrad' suggests the novelist Joseph Conrad, a red herring for the author.
explanation.definitionFit: Cranford is Elizabeth Gaskell's 1853 book about a small English town, written in Queen Victoria's reign.
